title: A Hox Code Gives Each Segment Its Identity

scenes.visual: Title: A Hox Code Gives Each Segment Its Identity. Show a hindbrain strip with distinct Hox combinations and jaw and face motor-neuron symbols.

scenes.tts: Why do similar-looking hindbrain segments make different neurons? Each segment carries an address written in Hox transcription factors. Its mix of Hox proteins, working with segment genes such as Krox twenty, helps set which neurons it makes and where their axons go. That matters for jaw and face movement. The small bulges are called rhombomeres. In chick, r two and r three make trigeminal motor neurons; r four and r five make facial motor neurons.

scenes.visual: Open on similar-looking rhombomeres. Immediately overlay different combinations of Hox marks and a Krox20 label, then connect them to neuron identity and axon paths. Map chick r2-r3 to trigeminal motor neurons and r4-r5 to facial motor neurons, with jaw and face symbols. Remove the pill opening.

scenes.tts: Test that address by removing Hox B one in mice. Normally, facial motor neurons are born in r four and migrate back to r six. Without Hox B one, r four loses parts of its identity. Its motor neurons fail to form or migrate normally; some behave like trigeminal neurons. The facial motor nucleus does not form normally. The segment is still there. What changes is what its cells become.

scenes.visual: Compare normal and Hoxb1 knockout mouse hindbrains. In normal, show r4-born facial motor neurons moving to r6. In knockout, retain the r4 segment outline, change part of its identity code toward r2, and show abnormal motor-neuron identity and migration with a failed facial motor nucleus. Label these as related mutant outcomes; do not depict every neuron as absent or converted.

scenes.tts: The addresses also sit in compartments. In chick, descendants of a cell labelled before boundaries appear can span neighbouring rhombomeres. Label a cell after boundaries appear, and its descendants stay within one. Cell sorting helps keep borders sharp. In fish and frog, Eph A four receptors and ephrin B ligands on neighbouring cells promote sorting at contact. These borders restrict progenitor mixing. Later neurons can still migrate, as the facial motor neurons do.

scenes.tts: What helps establish the Hox code? Retinoic acid, a product of vitamin A. Raldh two makes it in mesoderm beside the future hindbrain and spinal cord. Cyp twenty-six enzymes destroy it, with Cyp twenty-six A one strongly expressed toward the front. Like a bath with a tap and drain, supply behind and destruction in front leave more signal at the back and less at the front.

scenes.visual: Introduce retinoic acid as an input to the Hox code already established. Show Raldh2 synthesis in adjacent mesoderm and Cyp26 degradation, highlighting anterior Cyp26a1. Use the tap-and-drain analogy to show a posterior-high, anterior-low signal; keep Hox and segment-regulator labels visible.

scenes.tts: Retinoic acid reaches the nucleus and binds R A R. This receptor works with R X R on short DNA sequences called retinoic acid response elements. Hox A one and Hox B one carry these elements. Retinoic acid helps switch on the front-most Hox genes, working alongside F G F and Wnt signals.

scenes.visual: Show retinoic acid binding RAR, paired with RXR at a retinoic acid response element beside Hoxa1 and Hoxb1. Show activation as one input within a network; add FGF and Wnt as parallel signals rather than making a static gradient the whole identity mechanism.

scenes.tts: Change this input and the code moves. In mouse embryos exposed to extra retinoic acid early, Hox domains changed. Rhombomeres two and three shifted toward the identity of four and five. The signal helps set regional identity.

scenes.tts: The chromosome carries an order too. Hox genes at the three prime end reach farthest forward along the body. Genes toward the five prime end have front edges farther back. In mouse and chick, three prime genes also switch on first, and five prime genes later. This is colinearity: chromosome order matches position and timing along the growing body.
